title: Why industry took off in Britain, not China
place: Western Europe and Asia (Qing China, Mughal India, Tokugawa Japan)
summary: Western Europe and its settler colonies came to outpace Qing China, Mughal India and Tokugawa Japan. When this 'Great Divergence' began, and why, remains disputed.
why: It asks why the modern industrial world began where and when it did.

notes.problem: Evidence misattributes: page cites Maddison only as an external link and the 1400 claim to a 2014 study; van Zanden's point is that late-18th-century living standards in advanced Asia were COMPARABLE, the opposite of the proposal.

question: Why did Western Europe, led by Britain, industrialise and outpace China and other advanced Asian economies?
evidence: Broadberry finds England's silver wages three times the Yangzi Delta's by 1600; Pomeranz and the California school argue the most advanced parts of Asia were comparable until the 19th century.
wouldSettle: Comparable long-run wage, income and output series for England and the Yangzi Delta accepted by both camps.

theories.name: Coal and colonies
theories.idea: Pomeranz: nearby coal and New World land let Britain escape land limits; critics say coal was substitutable.

theories.name: High wages, cheap energy
theories.idea: Allen: high British wages made labour-saving machines pay.

theories.name: Institutions and property rights
theories.idea: Europe's property and commercial law were more secure; Pomeranz counters that China's land market was freer.

theories.name: Ideas and competing states
theories.idea: Mokyr's market for ideas and rivalry among fragmented states (Cox, Sng; Diamond on geography) restrained rulers.
